book.title: Building Projects with AI
book.subtitle: From clear requests to judgment, verification and delivery
book.audience: People who have tried AI coding but lack an overview of project development. No prior Python, Git or terminal experience is required.
book.baseline: Tool-neutral, using a personal study-list webpage throughout. Practice decisions in the book, then work in a separate directory. Commands use Git 2.28+ and Node.js 22.12+ capabilities; QA.md records the actual verification environment.
outcomes: Turn an idea into a user scenario, first-release scope and acceptance cases
Explain the roles of files, data, browsers and servers
Make focused Git commits and distinguish local commits, pushes, PRs and deployment
Give an agent accurate context and tasks, then inspect important changes
Use reproduction, boundary cases and requirements to judge results
Deliver a runnable small project with backups, recovery and clear limitations
outOfScope: Full algorithms and language training for professional engineering
Implementation of realtime collaboration, payments, authentication or production databases
Cloud account registration, paid service selection and automatic deployment
Advanced Git history rewriting, complex rebases and merge-commit reverts
Guaranteed prompt outcomes, arbitrary code execution or runtime model services

questions.problem: Turn build an amazing study tool with every feature into a first release.
questions.hint: Return to one person's specific difficulty.
questions.answer: User: yourself. Scenario: finding plans in the evening. First release: add, complete, delete and save. Accounts and synchronization are deferred.
solution: Identify the user and purpose.
Keep features needed for the complete workflow.
Write criteria for ordinary input, whitespace and refresh.

questions.problem: How do you verify creation works?
questions.answer: From an empty list, submitting Learn Git creates an unfinished item; whitespace creates nothing; surrounding whitespace is trimmed.
solution: State the successful result.
State rejected input.
Make results observable, rather than merely absence of an error.

questions.problem: Trace one addition and explain the server's role.
questions.hint: Distinguish file delivery from business-data persistence.
questions.answer: Input → app.mjs event → tasks.mjs rules → localStorage → rendering. server.mjs serves static files only.
solution: Read entry-point references.
Follow submission to validation and saving.
Confirm there is no shared-list API.

questions.problem: npm start fails. What information should the agent receive?
questions.answer: Current directory, tool versions, command and complete error; relevant configuration if needed.
solution: Check the environment against instructions.
Distinguish directory, tools and port failures.
Do not delete dependency records casually.

questions.problem: HEAD v1, index v2, working tree v3: what does committing and pushing share?
questions.hint: Push shares commits, not the working tree directly.
questions.answer: The commit records v2 and the remote branch receives it; v3 remains local unstaged work.
solution: Commit reads staged content.
Push transfers branch history.
Sharing v3 requires reviewing, staging, committing and pushing it.

questions.problem: Distinguish unstaging, discarding edits and reversing a pushed commit.
questions.answer: restore --staged keeps edits; ordinary restore overwrites unstaged working changes; revert can reverse an ordinary shared commit through a new record.
solution: Inspect status and diffs first.
Backup needed content.
Choose the matching operation and verify again.

questions.problem: Write a brief for fixing list loss after refresh.
questions.hint: Give current behavior, scope, criteria and evidence.
questions.answer: Require persistence; provide URL, steps, actual/expected results and save/load files. Diagnose first without adding synchronization. Request actual tests and browser evidence.
solution: Make the failure reproducible.
Constrain unrelated structural changes.
Deliver command results and verification gaps.

questions.problem: The agent changes 20 files for button color. How do you review?
questions.answer: Inspect files and diffs, ask why unrelated changes are necessary, reduce to styling scope and check keyboard and narrow screens.
solution: File count alone does not decide correctness.
Check whether data and dependency changes are necessary.
Record checks after acceptance.

questions.problem: Why do green automated tests not establish whole-site verification?
questions.answer: Rule tests do not exercise browser events, storage or layout. Perform relevant page checks and report gaps.
solution: List coverage.
Add normal, boundary and failure interaction checks.
Limit conclusions to actual evidence.

questions.problem: A backup is valid JSON but has invalid fields. What happens?
questions.answer: Reject the entire file without replacing the list. Validate version, fields, types, IDs and limits.
solution: Parse first.
Validate every record.
Write only after validity and confirmation.

questions.problem: What should a personal-list handoff include?
questions.hint: Let someone else run and understand it.
questions.answer: Source, runtime requirements, commands, version, acceptance evidence, limitations, backup/recovery instructions and deferred ideas.
solution: Prepare runnable materials.
Match the delivered version to checks.
Explain data location and restoration.

questions.problem: How should upgrading to multiuser synchronization begin?
questions.answer: Confirm separate/shared records, read/write permissions, conflicts and recovery, then rewrite scope and acceptance.
solution: An icon is not synchronization.
The original local-storage design has limits.
Build around confirmed scenarios.

exam.problem: Capstone: independently deliver a personal study list.
exam.answer: Deliver a one-page plan, at least 6 acceptance cases, data/file maps, 2 briefs, at least 3 focused commits, test and browser evidence, README and runnable source.
solution: Specify the user and first release, excluding synchronization.
Include ordinary creation, whitespace, duplicate titles, toggling, refresh and valid/invalid restoration.
Implement creation, manipulation, storage and handoff checkpoints, reviewing and checking each.
Compare with the appendix rather than merely copying; record unchecked environments and limits.

exam.problem: Evaluate: AI adds a cloud service and embeds a key in the webpage to change a button color.
exam.answer: Reject unrelated cloud services and client-side secrets. If exposed, revoke/rotate first. Return to styling scope and recheck.
solution: The change does not match the color task.
Read/edit permissions do not authorize a new external service.
Inspect diffs, lockfiles and artifacts; check keyboard and mobile layout.

exam.problem: Evaluate: tests were deleted, saving reports success, but refresh loses records.
exam.hint: Green results and success text can both mislead.
exam.answer: Do not accept. Restore requirement-based checks, reproduce and distinguish writing, reading and origin failures. Retest after fixing.
solution: Preserve errors and version evidence.
Do not hide exceptions to report success.
Judge completion against original criteria.

exam.problem: Evaluate: after pushing, the agent claims public deployment and synchronized user lists.
exam.hint: Separate remote code, deployment and user data.
exam.answer: Request accessible branch/PR, deployed URL and version evidence. localStorage does not provide multiuser synchronization; revisit the requirement.
solution: Push updates a target remote branch only.
A public page needs deployment and acceptance separately.
Shared user data needs additional architecture and permissions.

glossary.definition: An AI assistant that uses context and may operate tools. Capability does not authorize every operation.
A person's actions at a particular moment toward a goal, explaining a feature's purpose.
The essential complete workflow agreed for the current scenario, not every future idea.
Specific inputs, actions and expected outcomes for judging completion.
A command-entry and execution window. Its directory affects which files commands operate on.
Tools, versions, operating system and configuration required to run code.
An external package or tool whose versions and maintenance costs need management.
Records exact dependency resolution to support reproducible installation; do not delete reflexively on errors.
Where loading or execution begins, helping trace behavior through files.
Presentation and interaction in a client such as a browser.
The part commonly handling server-side data, permissions and business logic.
An agreed program interface specifying inputs, outputs and their meaning.
Origin-scoped browser string storage, subject to clearing, permissions and capacity.
Fields, types and relationships governing access, changes and validation.
A record's identity, distinct from a display title that may repeat.
Stores file-version history; distinct from the hosting website.
The file contents currently being edited.
Selected content for the next commit, potentially different from current files.
A local version snapshot and record, not created merely by saving a file.
The currently checked-out commit position, usually following the current branch tip.
A name pointing to a history tip, organizing changes by purpose.
A configured repository location; origin is a conventional name.
Update a target remote branch with local branch commits.
Review material proposing a merge into a target branch; not automatic merge or deployment.
Comparison of text changes between states, used to inspect scope and behavior.
An automatic merge cannot decide the result; understand both intentions and resolve explicitly.
This book's six-part collaboration material: goal, context, scope, acceptance, verification and delivery.
A test expression checking an expected condition.
After a fix, recheck existing behavior and relevant boundaries for unintended breakage.
A credential such as a key, token or password. Revoke or rotate after exposure.
Place runnable artifacts in the intended user-accessible environment.
Restore usable code or data state, treating each separately.

projectPlan.title: Checkpoint 1: record a plan
projectPlan.task: Build the page and creation rule. Ordinary input appears, whitespace is rejected; persistence is deferred.

projectPlan.title: Checkpoint 2: operate on the correct record
projectPlan.task: Toggle and delete by ID without affecting duplicate titles.
evidence: Check the remaining ID after deletion

projectPlan.title: Checkpoint 3: persist and restore
projectPlan.task: Refresh persistence, JSON backup and validated, confirmed restoration with failure feedback.
evidence: Restore IDs, titles and completion from a valid backup
Reject invalid backups without changing existing data

projectPlan.title: Checkpoint 4: enable a handoff
projectPlan.task: Complete README, acceptance records, version and known limits.
evidence: Run from instructions with another person or clean directory
Record local, remote and deployment states separately

lessons.title: Start with a real problem
lessons.subtitle: Replace an impressive-sounding product idea with an observable situation.
lessons.concept: Before building, identify who faces what difficulty, when it occurs, and what should improve.
lessons.intuition: If a friend asks for something tasty, you ask who is eating, where and with what constraints. Software needs that context too.
objectives: Describe one user, one moment and one specific difficulty.
State an observable sign that the problem has improved.

body.title: Start with a small inconvenience
body.text: Lin wants to study each evening but forgets yesterday's plan. The user is Lin; the moment is the start of study; the problem is plans buried in chats. Describe that before choosing buttons or technology. Wanting a cool website does not explain its purpose.

body.title: Describe actions, not feature names
body.text: Turn list management into actions: enter a plan and add it; mark it complete; delete it when no longer needed. These actions suggest a simple page. You need not know the code yet, but each action needs a purpose.

body.title: Give the agent a checkable starting point
body.text: Ask the agent to identify missing information, while choosing the intended user yourself. Whether plans survive refresh matters here. Whether to add particle effects does not solve the missing-plan problem.

formalDefinition.text: Before building, identify who faces what difficulty, when it occurs, and what should improve.
conditions: For small personal learning projects. In shared repositories, follow the team's conventions.
This method produces checkable evidence; it cannot guarantee arbitrary AI output is correct.

workflow: Describe one user, one moment and one specific difficulty.
List the actions needed to achieve the user's goal.
State an observable sign that the problem has improved.

workedExamples.title: From wish to scenario
workedExamples.problem: Rewrite: Build me an amazing learning tool.
steps: Choose yourself rather than every learner.
Identify difficulty finding plans before studying each day.
Define success as seeing unfinished plans on opening the page.
workedExamples.answer: Before studying each day, I want to find yesterday's plans. Build a study-list page where I can add plans, mark them complete and delete unwanted ones. Initially, only I will use it in my own browser.

workedExamples.title: Find missing requirements
workedExamples.problem: A friend wants a class-wide study list. Can you build it exactly like a personal list?
steps: Shared use means multiple readers and writers.
Ask whether lists are separate and whether people may edit others' items.
Agree on scope before discussing accounts and servers.
workedExamples.answer: Ask whether everyone shares one list, who may edit, and whether cross-device synchronization is required. These answers change the architecture; personal browser storage is not shared storage.

commonMistakes.claim: Choosing technology makes requirements clear.
commonMistakes.correction: A framework describes implementation, not the actions a user needs.

commonMistakes.claim: AI should infer my real intention.
commonMistakes.correction: Have it state assumptions and questions. Confirm answers that would change the project's direction.

practice.problem: Rewrite: I want a productivity tool, as a use scenario.
practice.hint: Add a user, moment and difficulty.
practice.answer: After dinner, I waste time searching chats for study plans. I want one page showing unfinished items.
solution: Choose yourself as the user.
Describe current behavior and friction instead of using efficient as a substitute for an observable change.

practice.problem: Is use React a user problem or an implementation choice?
practice.hint: A user can describe the goal without knowing a framework.
practice.answer: An implementation choice. A user problem might be plans disappearing after refresh.
solution: Separate the goal from the method.
Specify persistence before discussing how to implement it.

practice.problem: What is missing from a shared-list request?
practice.hint: Consider who may see and edit data.
practice.answer: Whether it is one shared list, who has editing rights, and whether synchronization and login are needed.
solution: List questions affecting permissions and data location.
Decide about a server after confirming the answers.

practice.problem: Give the simplest observable success for this example.
practice.hint: Use one action and one visible result.
practice.answer: After adding Practice Git, it appears in the list and can be found next time.
solution: The action is adding a plan.
The result is seeing and finding it again; later lessons specify persistence conditions.

learningCheck.question: Which statement is most useful before coding?
choices: Let me find unfinished plans each day
Use the most advanced technology stack
feedback: No concrete scenario makes completion hard to judge.
The user goal can now be broken into actions.
Technology still does not explain the problem.

interactiveVisual.prediction: Would you accept an agent's immediate suggestion of a leaderboard?

steps.question: The agent proposes building a leaderboard first. How do you respond?
choices: Ask how it helps me find my plans
feedback: This shifts the first release toward a different problem.
Relate the suggestion to the user goal before deciding.
Scope grows and verification becomes harder.

steps.question: The agent asks whether plans should survive refresh. What do you choose?
feedback: Finding tomorrow's plans depends on saving; answer explicitly.
Core behavior needs confirmed requirements.
Appearance does not answer the storage question.

steps.question: Which material is most useful to retain now?
choices: The user scenario and three essential actions
feedback: Rankings do not establish whether the user problem is solved.
These anchor scope and acceptance criteria.
Record future ideas separately so they do not obscure the first release.

interactiveVisual.followUp: Choose a real difficulty of your own. Describe its user, timing, actions and outcome.

lessons.title: Keep the first release finishable
lessons.subtitle: Validate the idea with one small, complete workflow.
lessons.concept: Build only enough to complete the initial scenario. Record other ideas for later.
lessons.intuition: Build a usable bicycle before deciding whether it needs a basket; do not commission an entire transport system at once.
objectives: List the essential features forming one complete workflow.
Attach an immediate check to each small change.

body.title: Draw the smallest complete workflow
body.text: For the study list: add a plan, see it, complete or delete it, then find it next time. Display and persistence are essential. Accounts, rankings, reminders and cross-device synchronization are deferred deliberately.

body.title: Separate now from later
body.text: Use two lists: required now and consider later. Ask of each requirement: without it, can the user still complete this scenario? If yes, defer it. Scope can change, but update the plan and acceptance criteria honestly.

body.title: Deliver one checkable change at a time
body.text: First show an empty list, then add items, then completion, then persistence. Each task needs a check. A single finish-the-site task postpones discovering unsuitable data or storage design. Small steps reveal errors early, not merely shorten prompts.

formalDefinition.text: Build only enough to complete the initial scenario. Record other ideas for later.
conditions: For small personal learning projects. In shared repositories, follow the team's conventions.
This method produces checkable evidence; it cannot guarantee arbitrary AI output is correct.

workflow: List the essential features forming one complete workflow.
Defer ideas unnecessary for that workflow.
Attach an immediate check to each small change.

workedExamples.title: Deciding about login
workedExamples.problem: Does a personal single-browser first release need login?
steps: The only user is you.
Cross-device sharing is not required.
Complete the scenario with local storage and state its limits.
workedExamples.answer: No login initially. Data stays in this browser and does not synchronize to other devices. If synchronization becomes necessary, redesign accounts and storage then.

workedExamples.title: Split a large task
workedExamples.problem: How would you divide finish the study list?
steps: Display the page and empty state first.
Add creation, completion and deletion, checking each action.
Then add persistence and backup, checking refresh and restoration.
workedExamples.answer: Task 1: empty list. Task 2: add nonblank plans and reject whitespace. Task 3: toggle and delete by ID. Task 4: refresh persistence and JSON backup. Verify each separately and fix failures before continuing.

commonMistakes.claim: More features make a better first release.
commonMistakes.correction: First establish that one workflow is useful; extras add delay and ambiguity.

commonMistakes.claim: Split tasks by files.
commonMistakes.correction: Prefer verifiable behaviors; one small behavior may touch several files.

practice.problem: Which comes first: reminders, rankings or adding plans?
practice.answer: Adding plans. The other two are not essential to a personal list.
solution: Make recording and retrieval work first.
Keep other ideas on the later list.

practice.problem: How should you explain the absence of cloud synchronization?
practice.hint: State what happens on another device.
practice.answer: Data is stored only in this browser. Changing devices or clearing storage will not restore it automatically; download a backup.
solution: Scope decisions affect user experience.
Put limitations in user-facing instructions, not just the development plan.

practice.problem: Turn finish the page into one small task.
practice.hint: Choose behavior you can verify by clicking.
practice.answer: Submitting a nonblank title adds an item; whitespace-only input gives a message without adding anything.
solution: Specify the triggering action.
Specify successful and invalid-input outcomes.

practice.problem: What if multiuser synchronization becomes mandatory midway?
practice.hint: It changes data location and permissions.
practice.answer: Revisit the plan, confirm sharing and permissions, rewrite scope and acceptance criteria, then estimate the new tasks.
solution: Recognize a requirements change.
Do not pretend a personal-list design only needs another button.

learningCheck.question: Which belongs in the first release?
choices: A personal list with automatic payments
Add, complete, delete and save locally
feedback: Payments add another business problem and risks.
This completes the original scenario with clear scope.
Several new scenarios make the first release harder to finish.

interactiveVisual.prediction: Four tempting additions are suggested. Which deserve inclusion now?

steps.question: The agent proposes accounts, but only you use the app.
choices: Defer them and explain local-storage limits
feedback: Accounts expand the first release.
Scope stays clear and the user understands its limits.
This breaks finding plans on a later day.

steps.question: Refreshing loses the list.
choices: Fix this gap in the first release
feedback: Persistence is part of the current scenario.
New features cannot repair a broken core workflow.
A title change does not prevent data loss.

steps.question: One change includes creation, login and payments. How should it be adjusted?
choices: Use a longer prompt for everything
Split it and verify creation first
feedback: A longer description does not reduce change scope.
Smaller changes are easier to understand and verify.
Reliability needs evidence.

interactiveVisual.followUp: Write required now and consider later lists for your project, explaining each choice.

lessons.title: Define what done means
lessons.subtitle: Turn useful into results you can check yourself.
lessons.concept: Acceptance criteria specify inputs, actions and expected outcomes so you and the agent share a definition of done.
lessons.intuition: Not too sweet is ambiguous when ordering a cake; size, flavor and delivery date are easier to check.
objectives: Specify the starting state, action and expected result.
Judge completion using your checks, not the agent's report alone.

body.title: Write a check in three parts
body.text: Use Given, When, Then. Given an empty list, when Practice Git is submitted, then one unfinished item appears. This specifies state, action and outcome. Define it before coding so the current implementation does not lower the requirement.

body.title: Boundary cases expose omissions
body.text: Normal input covers only the normal path. Check whitespace, duplicate titles, refresh and storage failure too. This first release allows duplicate titles with distinct IDs and rejects whitespace-only titles. After trimming, the limit is 80 UTF-16 code units; some symbols use more than one. JavaScript length is not a universal character count.

body.title: Separate behavior, experience and limits
body.text: Functional criteria describe results; experience criteria include keyboard submission and no mobile overflow. State that devices do not synchronize. Limits cannot excuse failing promised refresh persistence. Change goals only by revisiting the original purpose.

formalDefinition.text: Acceptance criteria specify inputs, actions and expected outcomes so you and the agent share a definition of done.
conditions: For small personal learning projects. In shared repositories, follow the team's conventions.
This method produces checkable evidence; it cannot guarantee arbitrary AI output is correct.

workflow: Specify the starting state, action and expected result.
Include at least one boundary or failure input.
Judge completion using your checks, not the agent's report alone.

workedExamples.title: Checking blank input
workedExamples.problem: How do you test that blank plans cannot be added?
steps: Start with an empty list.
Enter three spaces and submit.
Check unchanged count and an understandable message.
workedExamples.answer: Given zero items, submitting only spaces leaves zero items and displays Please enter a study plan. Checking that the button clicks is insufficient.

workedExamples.title: Checking duplicate titles
workedExamples.problem: Two items are titled Learn Git. What should deleting the second do?
steps: Create two same-title records.
Confirm distinct IDs.
Delete the second and check that the first remains.
workedExamples.answer: Only the first remains. Deletion targets the chosen record; allowed duplicate titles cannot identify records uniquely.

commonMistakes.claim: No page error means done.
commonMistakes.correction: Check inputs and results too; silent data loss may produce no visible error.

commonMistakes.claim: Green tests guarantee requirements are met.
commonMistakes.correction: If refresh or blank-input cases are missing, green results support only the cases that exist.

practice.problem: Write a criterion for completion toggling.
practice.hint: Specify the initial state and click outcome.
practice.answer: Given an unfinished item, checking it marks it complete; unchecking restores unfinished status.
solution: Define the first change.
Check reversal so completion is not one-way.

practice.problem: Make the requirement premium interface checkable.
practice.hint: Focus on reading, screen size and controls.
practice.answer: At 390px width, titles wrap without horizontal scrolling and every button is keyboard-focusable.
solution: Translate preferences into specific layout requirements.
Do not rely on premium as the only criterion.

practice.problem: What is missing from ordinary creation, deletion and completion checks?
practice.answer: Refresh persistence, whitespace rejection and deleting one of duplicate titles.
solution: Check the cross-day scenario.
Include invalid and ambiguous inputs, not just the happy path.

practice.problem: The agent reports tests passed. What else do you need?
practice.answer: Commands, actual results, covered cases and unchecked items, followed by your own key-action checks.
solution: Ask for evidence and scope.
One conclusion does not guarantee every feature.

learningCheck.question: Which criterion can you execute directly?
choices: Whitespace submission leaves the count unchanged and shows a message
feedback: No specific input or result.
The action and expected result can be checked directly.
Test count alone says nothing about coverage.

interactiveVisual.prediction: What does checking only normal input miss?

steps.question: What should happen after entering three spaces?
choices: Add nothing and show a message
feedback: A blank item expresses no plan.
This meets whitespace-rejection criteria.
Expected invalid inputs need handling and explanation.

steps.question: Deleting one of two same-title records removes both.
feedback: Allowed duplicates cannot all be deleted by title.
Use independent IDs to target the selected record.
Wording cannot fix incorrect data changes.

steps.question: All written tests pass, but none tests refresh.
choices: Record the gap and check refresh yourself
feedback: There is no evidence for that claim.
Complete the evidence for the cross-day workflow.
Do not lower the core goal to fit the implementation.

interactiveVisual.followUp: Choose a feature and write normal, boundary and failure acceptance cases.

lessons.title: Understand the project's files
lessons.subtitle: Find the entry point, then each file's responsibility.
lessons.concept: A project is a set of cooperating files. Start with README, then trace entry points to interface, logic, configuration and tests.
lessons.intuition: A restaurant has a menu, kitchen and accounts. Mixing them on one sheet makes changes difficult.
objectives: Read README and configuration to find entry points and commands.
Trace one user action through its files; do not delete unfamiliar files casually.

body.title: Start with instructions
body.text: Read README for purpose, setup and limitations. In a Node project, package.json defines scripts as command aliases and dependencies as external packages. This example has none; other web projects may require installation.

body.title: Trace four kinds of files
body.text: index.html supplies structure and loads style.css and app.mjs. CSS controls appearance. app.mjs connects controls to data; tasks.mjs defines creation, toggling and deletion; tasks.test.mjs tests those rules. server.mjs serves files locally, and README explains operation. Identify responsibilities before choosing frameworks.

body.title: Read enough to explain behavior
body.text: You need not understand every syntax detail yet. Know who receives input, validates it, saves it and redraws the page. Ask the agent to explain a line with concrete input and compare its explanation with the file. Why is ID checked before deletion? is more verifiable than explain everything.

formalDefinition.text: A project is a set of cooperating files. Start with README, then trace entry points to interface, logic, configuration and tests.
conditions: For small personal learning projects. In shared repositories, follow the team's conventions.
This method produces checkable evidence; it cannot guarantee arbitrary AI output is correct.

workflow: Read README and configuration to find entry points and commands.
Identify interface, logic, tests and tooling files.

workedExamples.title: Change appearance only
workedExamples.problem: Where should you look to enlarge buttons?
steps: Find button rules in CSS.
Check button structure and classes in HTML and JavaScript.
Check narrow screens and keyboard operation afterward.
workedExamples.answer: Primarily style.css; inspect index.html and app.mjs as needed. Button size does not require changing data structures or deleting tests.

workedExamples.title: Change the title limit
workedExamples.problem: Where does changing the limit from 80 to 100 have consequences?
steps: tasks.mjs contains the validation constant.
Tests cover boundaries 80 and 81.
Instructions and feedback mention the limit too.
workedExamples.answer: Confirm the requirement, then update the rule, boundary tests and README together. Changing only the message leaves actual validation at 80.

commonMistakes.claim: Delete unfamiliar files to simplify the project.
commonMistakes.correction: Check references and purpose first. Configuration, lockfiles and tests may be essential.

commonMistakes.claim: If AI can edit, I need not know the entry point.
commonMistakes.correction: Knowing entry points helps judge whether changes fit the goal and diagnose failures.

practice.problem: What do CSS and tasks.mjs control?
practice.answer: CSS controls styling. tasks.mjs defines creation, toggling, deletion and backup format.
solution: Remember responsibilities rather than extensions alone.
Test rule changes; inspect the page for style changes.

practice.problem: How do you find what npm start runs?
practice.answer: Inspect scripts.start in package.json; here it is node server.mjs.
solution: Command aliases vary by project.
Do not assume every start script does the same thing.

lessons.subtitle: Understand the working tree, staging area and commits.
lessons.concept: Saving changes the working tree. git add stages the content at that moment. git commit records staged content locally.

body.title: Know which repository you are in
body.text: Git records versions; GitHub can host repositories. In a new practice directory, git init -b main creates a repository. Use git clone for an existing remote project; do not casually initialize inside another repository. Start with git status. Repository-local user.name and user.email set commit identity here; a public commit can expose that email.

body.title: Three versions can differ
body.text: The working tree holds current files; the index stages the next commit; HEAD identifies the checked-out commit, usually the branch tip. After git add README.md, later edits do not update its staged version. git diff compares working tree with index; git diff --staged compares index with HEAD. New unstaged files normally need status and direct inspection too.

body.title: Give each commit one purpose
body.text: Read diffs, run relevant checks and stage explicit files before committing. Describe the reason, such as reject whitespace-only plans. .gitignore prevents ordinary addition of matching untracked files, including dependencies and local secrets. It neither removes tracked content nor erases leaked history.

lessons.title: Branches, pushes and pull requests
lessons.subtitle: Give a change a place and a review process.
lessons.concept: A branch maintains a line of history, push updates a remote branch, and a PR proposes merging changes into another branch. None automatically means deployment.
lessons.intuition: Revising your own draft, sending it out and asking an editor to accept it are different steps.
objectives: Check the working tree before creating a branch for one change.
Explain the trigger, changed behavior and verification in a PR; distinguish commit, push, merge and release.

body.title: One focused branch
body.text: From a clean working tree, git switch -c feature/empty-title creates and switches branches. Commits there do not advance main automatically. Branches are not isolated folders: uncommitted changes may follow a switch or prevent it. Inspect status and preserve work first.

body.title: A remote is another repository location
body.text: git remote -v shows configured names and URLs. origin is conventional, not a fixed service. git push -u origin feature/empty-title uploads that branch and sets its upstream. You need permission; without it, commonly fork first and open a PR from your fork. Use supported authentication rather than source-code credentials.

body.title: A PR is a proposal with evidence
body.text: State the original triggering input, old and new behavior, changed files, checks and limits. Reviewers inspect diffs and request changes. PR creation, passing checks and merging are separate states. Website updates depend on build and release configuration; some projects deploy manually.

body.title: First sharing and later updates
body.text: A repository initialized from a ZIP has no origin. Create your own empty hosted repository and pass its actual URL to git remote add origin. For existing projects, git clone the real URL and follow README. Before updates inspect status and preserve local work. git fetch origin downloads records without merging. With upstream set and a clean tree, git pull --ff-only accepts only fast-forwards. If histories diverge, inspect both and follow project conventions; do not hide divergence with force-push.

lessons.title: Identify what you need to undo
lessons.subtitle: Different kinds of recovery need different operations.
lessons.concept: Distinguish unstaging, discarding working edits, reversing commits and resolving conflicts before choosing an undo operation.
lessons.intuition: Removing a draft from an envelope, discarding a desk copy and sending a correction have different costs.
objectives: Inspect working tree, index and log to identify the state being undone.

body.title: Inspect before clearing
body.text: Start with git status, git diff and git diff --staged. git restore --staged README.md unstages while preserving edits. git restore README.md overwrites unstaged edits from the index; preserve anything needed first. Git may not recover never-recorded drafts. Do not reflexively use reset --hard or clean -fd.

body.title: Correct shared history with a new commit
body.text: For an ordinary shared commit, git revert creates a reverse commit while retaining history. Start clean and identify the correct commit. Revert may conflict; merge-commit reversal is beyond scope. stash temporarily saves work, excluding untracked files unless -u is specified. Applying it can conflict; it is not permanent backup.

body.title: Understand both sides of a conflict
body.text: When branches edit the same area differently, Git may need a decision. Read requirements and both intentions, write the final content, remove markers, test, stage and complete the operation. Do not randomly choose ours or theirs. To stop, use the abort command appropriate to the active merge or revert, after inspecting status.

body.title: Give records a clear shape
body.text: Each record has id, title and done: identity, readable text and completion state. Backups wrap tasks in a versioned object. Versions identify formats. body.title: Local storage can fail

body.title: Prepare the delivery materials
body.text: README should explain tools, commands, scope and limits. Match commits and version notes to actual checks. Projects with dependencies install from lockfiles and build. This example needs no bundling: publish index.html, style.css, app.mjs and tasks.mjs. Tests and the local server are not browser entry files.

body.title: Recheck the public URL
body.text: A development server is local. Deployment puts runnable artifacts in the target environment. At the real URL, check resource requests, actions, keyboard, narrow screens and saving. Localhost records do not migrate to the new origin. Hosting paths vary; follow the target's instructions. This book does not create hosting accounts or buy services for readers.

body.title: Separate code and data recovery
body.text: Record the previous working code and publication procedure. Restore a usable artifact and verify it after failure. Old code may not understand new data; format changes need backup and migration planning. Even without upgrades, this example's restoration replaces records. Keep an error-reporting route after release.

body.title: Write your own plan first
body.text: Use the study list without reading the reference implementation initially. Write scenario, now/later scope, file responsibilities, data fields and acceptance cases. Give the agent one small task brief. The reference is a comparison, not proof of your understanding. Explain each step's purpose and check yourself.

body.title: Progress through checkpoints
body.text: Checkpoint 1: page and creation. 2: completion and deletion. 3: persistence and backup. 4: tests, diagnosis and instructions. At each, review diffs, run checks, inspect the browser and commit. Suggestions for chat, payments or synchronization should be judged against agreed scope, not novelty.

body.title: Use explanation to find the next lesson
body.text: Have another person run README. Explain where data lives, what commit records, why blanks are rejected, how to diagnose refresh loss, who sees data and which cases remain unchecked. Revisit lessons you cannot explain. This framework supports small projects; further study of programming, HTTP, data and security remains valuable.

workedExamples.title: Choose the next step
workedExamples.problem: After a personal list, should you add search or multiuser synchronization?
steps: Ask whether the problem is finding many items or actually sharing them.
Search extends local filtering; synchronization changes data location and permissions.

workedExamples.answer: For many hard-to-find plans, add search and test empty queries, case handling and completed items. For genuine sharing, design permissions and conflicts first; this is not an equally small change.
